🎬 Chaptered Timeline: “The App Store Antitrust Shockwave”

In this chart-race video, we track how antitrust pressure and payment rule changes from EU/UK/US regulators rippled through the biggest mobile storefronts—while one gaming publisher got instantly punished.

00:00 — The setup: Apple’s App Store economy scales (2012–2015)
03:10 — Epic’s Fortnite era starts to matter (2016–2018)
06:20 — The “payments & rules” fight becomes inevitable (2019)
08:40 — 2020 pivot: Apple App Store friction + enforcement escalates
11:30 — 2021–2022: Antitrust hits—Apple faces court pressure; outcomes change store behavior
14:10 — The shock moment: Epic’s Fortnite battle and forced disruption (2020–2022)
17:30 — 2023–2025: New rules, new workarounds, new revenue splits
20:10 — 2026 line: estimated continuation for the race

📈 What you’re watching:
• Apple and Google both keep expanding App Store/Play billing revenue, but under more constraints.
• Epic’s at-stake storefront revenue drops sharply after the Epic vs Apple confrontation and changes in distribution/payments.
• Amazon Appstore remains comparatively small but steady.

instagram_caption:
🚀 The $100B App-Store Fight Nobody Thought Would Hit THIS Hard

Picture the mobile internet before the courtroom drama: one gatekeeper sells the route, developers pay the toll, and everyone builds inside the walled garden. Then the antitrust shockwave hits—fast, public, and brutal. In this timeline comparison, we’re watching revenue at stake swing like a needle while regulators force payment and distribution rule changes across Apple’s iOS App Store, Google Play, and Amazon Appstore—and while Epic Games takes the most visible hit.

Apple’s estimated App Store economics climb steadily from single-digit billions in the mid-2010s to about $22B by 2022. But the real story isn’t just growth—it’s the pressure. By 2021–2022, antitrust scrutiny intensifies across the EU and UK, and Apple begins absorbing the cost of compliance while still defending its platform. In 2025, the estimated Apple storefront revenue at stake is around $31B, with a 2026 projection of ~$33B.

Now look at Epic Games (Fortnite). Epic’s at-stake storefront revenue surges as Fortnite becomes a platform-wide phenomenon—rising from near-zero early on to around $6.5B at its peak in 2021. Then the shock: the Epic-vs-Apple confrontation and subsequent distribution/payment disruptions slam the numbers. By 2022–2025, Epic’s at-stake storefront revenue drops to about $3.9B (2023), then $2.6B (2025). The “enemy” didn’t just block— it rewired what was possible.

Meanwhile, Google Play keeps growing too, hitting about $20.5B by 2022 and roughly $26.0B by 2025. Amazon Appstore stays small but steady, hovering around ~$2.0B by 2025.

So here’s the question for you: If regulators forced TRUE side-loading everywhere tomorrow, who would win first—Apple’s App Store, Google Play, or the long-shot challengers?

facebook_caption:
The mobile app economy is often described as “just software,” but antitrust enforcement proved it’s also a power map. This timeline comparison visualizes the revenue at stake across major mobile storefronts—Apple’s App Store, Google Play, Amazon Appstore—and Epic Games (Fortnite), which became the most visible casualty of store-rule conflict.

From the mid-2010s onward, Apple’s estimated App Store revenue at stake rises from a few billions into the $20B+ range by 2022, even as regulators intensify scrutiny. The critical inflection occurs in 2020–2022: the combination of payment-rule pressure and platform litigation reshapes developer behavior and storefront economics. Epic’s Fortnite-related at-stake revenue climbs into the billions (peaking around ~$6.5B in 2021) before dropping sharply after the high-profile confrontation and the resulting distribution/payment disruptions.

Google Play shows steadier growth, reaching approximately $20.5B by 2022 and ~$26.0B by 2025, while Amazon Appstore remains comparatively smaller, moving around ~$2.0B by 2025. The chart’s ending illustrates how compliance-driven changes can slow one player’s upside while still allowing large platforms to keep monetizing distribution.

What do you think happens next: do storefront revenues consolidate even harder, or does real policy change unlock new winners?
